plan: [No prior rounds to learn from. With 5 bidders and third-price payment, the third-order statistic of five uniform draws has mean ~24.5, so bidding my true value is a safe, near-optimal strategy: it wins when the third-highest is below my value and avoids overbidding risk that could produce negative payoff. I will bid my private value to maximize expected surplus while keeping downside limited.]

[Third-price auction with 5 bidders incentivizes systematic overbidding. Assume symmetric linear bids b(v)=αv. With 4 opponents, probability win if bidding as-if t is t^4 and expected third-price (second-highest of 4 others) conditional on max<t is (3/5)t, so payoff ∝ t^4(v - α*(3/5)t). First-order condition gives best-response t=4v/(3α). Symmetry implies α=4/3, so equilibrium b(v)=(4/3)v. For v=$28, bid = (4/3)*28 = $37.333…, round to nearest $0.1 = $37.3.]

[With no past data, assume opponents bid near their values. In a 3rd‑price auction with independent uniform values, bidding my true value is a safe, simple strategy: it wins exactly when my value is highest and yields positive expected surplus (approx 0.4·v conditional on winning). Overbidding risks winning when others' values exceed mine and paying a high 3rd‑price; underbidding risks losing profitable wins. With v = $24, I bid my value to capture expected positive profit while avoiding excess risk.]

[This is a 5-bidder, third-price auction (winner pays the 3rd-highest bid). No prior history to learn from and values redraw each round. There is no dominant strategy; overbidding risks paying more than my value while underbidding loses profitable wins. To maximize long-run payoff given uncertainty, I will bid my true value ($20) to avoid negative surplus while keeping reasonable chance to win when opponents' bids are lower.]

[Use the symmetric equilibrium for a third-price auction with n=5: optimal bid = (n-1)/(n-2) * value = 4/3 * v. For v=47 this equals 62.666..., so bid the nearest $0.1, 62.7, to maximize expected profit given independent draws.]
